concepts.title: Phong reflection model
concepts.one_liner: The Phong reflection model assumes the reflected light has ambient, diffuse (Lambertian), and specular components.
concepts.content:
A widely used model of surfaces with a specular component of reflection is the Phong reflection model @Phong1975. The light reflected from a surface is assumed to have three components that result in the observed reflection: (1) an ambient component, which is a constant term added to all reflections; (2) a diffuse component, which is the Lambertian reflection of @eq-Lambert; and (3) a specular reflection component. For a given ray direction, $\mathbf{q}$, from the surface, the Phong specular contribution, $\ell_{\mbox{Phong spec}}$, is:
$$\ell_{\mbox{Phong spec}} = k_s (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{q})^\alpha \ell_{\texttt{in}},$$
where $k_s$ is a constant, $\alpha$ is a parameter governing the spread of the specular reflection, and the unit vector $\mathbf{r}$ denotes the direction of maximum specular reflection, given by
$$\mathbf{r} = 2(\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{n} - \mathbf{p}$$
concepts.motivation_md: The Phong reflection model explains how surfaces reflect light with ambient, diffuse, and specular components, enabling realistic rendering of shiny and matte surfaces.
concepts.recap_md:
- Phong model includes ambient, diffuse (Lambertian), and specular reflection.
- Specular component $\ell_{\mbox{Phong spec}} = k_s (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{q})^\alpha \ell_{\texttt{in}}$.
- $\mathbf{r}$ is the direction of maximum specular reflection.

concepts.title: pinhole camera

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: A pinhole camera uses a small hole and a projection surface to create an image by allowing light from only one direction to reach each point on the surface.
concepts.content: Perhaps the simplest camera is a pinhole camera. A pinhole camera requires a light-tight enclosure, a small hole that lets light pass, and a projection surface where one senses or views the illumination intensity as a function of position. @fig-wallpicture (b) shows the geometry of a scene, the pinhole, and a projection surface (wall). For any given point on the projection surface, the light that falls there comes from only from one direction, along the straight line joining the surface position and the pinhole. This creates an image of what's in the world on the projection plane.
concepts.motivation_md: The pinhole camera model explains how a simple aperture projects a scene onto a surface, foundational for understanding image formation in cameras.
concepts.recap_md:
- A pinhole camera uses a small hole and a projection surface.
- Light at each point on the projection surface comes from one direction.
- This setup creates an image of the world on the projection plane.

concepts.title: World coordinates

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: World coordinates are a 3D Cartesian system with the camera's pinhole as origin and the Z axis perpendicular to the camera's sensing plane.
concepts.content: - World coordinates. Let the origin of a World Cartesian coordinate system be the camera's pinhole. The coordinates of 3D position of a point, $\mathbf{P}$, in the world will be $\mathbf{P} = (X, Y, Z)$, where the Z axis is perpendicular to the camera's sensing plane (projection plane).
concepts.motivation_md: World coordinates provide a fixed 3D reference frame to describe points relative to the camera, essential for mapping and projection.
concepts.recap_md:

- Coordinates are $\mathbf{P} = (X,Y,Z)$.
- Z axis is perpendicular to the camera's sensing plane.

concepts.title: Camera coordinates

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: Camera coordinates in the virtual camera plane are radially symmetrical to the projection plane and share the same sign as world coordinates.
concepts.content: - Camera coordinates in the virtual camera plane. The camera projection plane is behind the pinhole and at a distance $f$ of the origin. Let the coordinates in the camera projection plane, $x$ and $y$, be parallel to the world coordinate axes $X$ and $Y$ but in opposite directions, respectively. For simplicity, it is useful to create a virtual camera plane that is radially symmetrical to the projection plane with respect to the origin and it is placed in front of the camera (\[a\]). This virtual camera plane will create a projected image without the inversion of the image. The coordinates in the virtual camera plane will have the same sign as the world coordinates, that is, with the same $x$,$y$ coordinates (i.e., both images are identical apart from a flip).
concepts.motivation_md: Virtual camera coordinates simplify image analysis by avoiding inversion and aligning with world coordinates, making projections easier to interpret.
concepts.recap_md:
- Camera projection plane is behind the pinhole at distance $f$.
- Coordinates $x,y$ are parallel but opposite in direction to $X,Y$.
- Virtual camera plane in front avoids image inversion and matches world coordinate signs.

concepts.title: perspective projection

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: Equations called the perspective projection equations describe how distant objects become smaller through inverse scaling by $Z$.
concepts.content:
Equations @eq-perspctiveProj1 and @eq-perspctiveProj are called the **perspective projection equations**. Under perspective projection, distant objects become smaller through inverse scaling by $Z$. As we will see, the perspective projection equations apply not just to pinhole cameras but to most lens-based cameras and human vision as well.

![Perspective projection equations derived geometrically. From similar triangles, we have $x/f = X/Z$ and $y/f = Y/Z$. Similar triangles are indicated by the same color.](figures/imaging/similar_triangles2.png){#fig-pinholeGeometry2 width="80%"}
concepts.motivation_md: Perspective projection models how objects appear smaller as they get farther away, which is essential for understanding camera images and human vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- Perspective projection equations relate image coordinates to 3D coordinates scaled inversely by depth $Z$.
- Distant objects appear smaller due to this inverse scaling.
- Applies to pinhole cameras, lens-based cameras, and human vision.

concepts.title: orthographic projection

position.section_title: The Pinhole Camera and Image Formation

concepts.one_liner: Orthographic projection is an alternative to perspective projection where object size is independent of distance to the camera.
concepts.content:
An alternative to perspective projection is **orthographic projection**. @fig-orthographics shows the geometric interpretation of orthographic (or parallel) projection.

(see figure: Orthographic projection. Projection is done by parallel rays orthogonal to the projection plane. In this example, we have $x = X$ and $y = Y$.)

In this projection, as the rays are orthogonal to the projection plane, the size of objects is independent of the distance to the camera. The projection equations are generally written as follows: 
$$\begin{aligned}
x &= k X \nonumber \\
y &= k Y
\end{aligned}
$$

Orthographic projection is a good model for telephoto lenses, where the apparent size of objects in the image is roughly independent of their distance to the camera. We used this projection when building the simple visual system in @sec-simplesystem.

Orthographic Projection is a correct model when looking at an infinitely far away object that is infinitely zoomed in, as discussed in @sec-simplesystem.

concepts.recap_md:
- Orthographic projection uses parallel rays orthogonal to the projection plane.
- Object size in the image is independent of distance to the camera.
- Projection equations: $x = kX$, $y = kY$.

concepts.title: Lambertian Surfaces
concepts.one_liner: The Lambertian model approximates diffuse reflection with a simple BRDF where outgoing intensity depends on surface orientation and reflectance.
concepts.content:
In general, BRDFs can be quite complicated (see @Matusik2002), describing both diffuse and specular components of reflection. Even surfaces with completely diffuse reflections can give complicated reflectance distributions @Oren1994. A useful approximation describing diffuse reflection is the Lambertian model, with a particularly simple BRDF, which we denote as $F_L$. The outgoing ray intensity, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$, is a function only of the surface orientation relative to the incoming and outgoing ray directions, the wavelength, a scalar surface reflectance, and the incoming light power:
$$
\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F_{L} \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}} (\lambda), \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p} \right)  = a \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) \left( \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p} \right),
$$ {#eq-lambert}

where $a$ is the surface reflectance, or albedo, $\mathbf{n}$ is the surface normal vector, and $\mathbf{p}$ points toward the source of the incident light. Note that the brightness of the outgoing light ray depends on the orientation of the surface relative to the incident ray, as well as the reflectance, $a$, of the surface. For a Lambertian surface, the intensity of the reflected light is a function of the direction of the incoming light ray, but not a function of the outgoing direction of the ray, $\mathbf{q}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The Lambertian model simplifies complex surface reflectance by assuming purely diffuse reflection, making it easier to analyze and simulate light reflection.
concepts.recap_md:
- BRDFs describe complex reflection including diffuse and specular components.
- Lambertian model approximates diffuse reflection with a simple BRDF $F_L$.
- Outgoing intensity depends on surface reflectance $a$, surface normal $\mathbf{n}$, and incoming light direction $\mathbf{p}$.

slots.motivation: The Lambertian model simplifies complex surface reflectance by assuming purely diffuse reflection, making it easier to analyze and simulate light reflection.
slots.key_passage:

- Outgoing intensity depends on surface reflectance $a$, surface normal $\mathbf{n}$, and incoming light direction $\mathbf{p}$.

Note that the brightness of the outgoing light ray depends on the orientation of the surface relative to the incident ray, as well as the reflectance, $a$, of the surface. For a Lambertian surface, the intensity of the reflected light is a function of the direction of the incoming light ray, but not a function of the outgoing direction of the ray, $\mathbf{q}$.

key_passage.text: A useful approximation describing diffuse reflection is the **Lambertian model**, with a particularly simple BRDF, which we denote as $F_L$. The outgoing ray intensity, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$, is a function only of the surface orientation relative to the incoming and outgoing ray directions, the wavelength, a scalar surface reflectance, and the incoming light power: $$ \ell_{\texttt{out}} = F_{L} \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}} (\lambda), \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p} \right) = a \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) \left( \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p} \right), $$ where $a$ is the surface **reflectance**, or **albedo**, $\mathbf{n}$ is the surface normal vector, and $\mathbf{p}$ points toward the source of the incident light.

prereq.rationale: Understanding the bidirectional reflection distribution function (BRDF) requires the concept of a light ray, as the BRDF describes how light rays reflect off surfaces depending on their directions and properties.
The concept of reflectance or albedo is defined within the context of Lambertian surfaces, describing the scalar surface reflectance parameter used in the Lambertian BRDF model.
The Phong reflection model includes a diffuse component that is the Lambertian reflection, so understanding the Phong model requires knowledge of Lambertian surfaces and their BRDF.
The Phong reflection model builds on the general concept of BRDFs to model specular and diffuse reflection components, thus requiring understanding of BRDFs.
The Phong reflection model describes light reflected from surfaces in terms of light rays' directions and intensities, so it requires understanding the abstraction of light rays.
World coordinates are defined relative to the pinhole camera's origin, so understanding the pinhole camera is prerequisite.
Camera coordinates are defined in relation to world coordinates, so understanding world coordinates is necessary first.
Image coordinates relate to camera coordinates via an affine transform, so camera coordinates are prerequisite.
Perspective projection equations are derived using the concept of similar triangles.
Perspective projection equations apply to pinhole cameras, so understanding pinhole cameras is prerequisite.
The straw camera produces an orthographic projection image, so understanding orthographic projection is prerequisite.

overlay.rationale: Lambertian surfaces are a special case of BRDFs, representing a simplified model of diffuse reflection with a particularly simple BRDF function.
Orthographic projection is an alternative to perspective projection used in pinhole cameras, contrasting their projection methods.
Orthographic and perspective projections are different projection models; contrasting them aids understanding.
